title: The Lethal Trifecta: Designing Agents That Survive Prompt Injection
summary: Why filters and guardrail models fail against adaptive attackers, and how the Rule of Two, six design patterns and Google DeepMind's CaMeL make prompt injection structurally harmless instead. Ends with a concrete audit Lucas can run on his own agents, including this podcast pipeline, this week.
shownotes:
The threat model: no separate channel for instructions and data, and Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (private data, untrusted content, external communication)
Why detection fails: 'The Attacker Moves Second' broke 12 published defences with adaptive attacks, most above 90% success
Meta's Agents Rule of Two: at most two of untrusted input, sensitive data, and state change or external communication per session
Six design patterns for securing LLM agents: Action-Selector, Plan-Then-Execute, LLM Map-Reduce, Dual LLM, Code-Then-Execute, Context-Minimization
CaMeL: privileged and quarantined LLMs, capability tags and security policies; 77% vs 84% task success, about 2.8x tokens
Adaptive evaluation of out-of-band defences: an early, small-scale data point
OS-level containment: Claude Code sandboxing, network proxy allowlists and 84% fewer permission prompts; approval fatigue
Context: another OpenAI safety departure and the call for multiple layers of redundancy
Practical audit: Rule of Two on the Morning Signal pipeline, Map-Reduce feed triage, hooks plus sandbox, planted injection tests
